label: Mali Empire
pitch:
Sundiata Keita founds Mali Empire in 1235 after an epic victory, and within a century Mansa Musa would become possibly the richest person who ever lived. When Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca rolled through Cairo in 1324 with 60,000 attendants and tons of gold, Musa crashes Egyptian gold market for over a decade. Meanwhile, Timbuktu becomes center of learning with one of the medieval world's great libraries.

🔑 Key Facts:
• The Epic of Sundiata, preserved by the Griot oral tradition, is one of Africa's greatest literary works
• The Catalan Atlas depicts Mansa Musa holding a gold nugget — proof that Mali's fame reached European mapmakers
• Ibn Battuta visits Mali in 1352 and recorded detailed observations of its justice system and social customs
• The Sankore Mosque and University housed thousands of students studying theology, law, and astronomy

🤔 Why It Matters: Mali's Timbuktu manuscript tradition — hundreds of thousands of handwritten books on science, law, and history — demolishes the myth that sub-Saharan Africa had no written intellectual tradition.

🎲 Wild Card: Mali controls gold mines that produced so much of the precious metal that the Trans-Saharan salt-gold trade literally exchanged gold for salt pound-for-pound — because in the Sahara, salt was worth its weight in gold.

spans.label: Ghana Empire (Wagadu) predecessor
spans.description: The Ghana Empire — known to its own people as Wagadu — controlled the western Sahel gold-and-salt trade for roughly five centuries before its collapse opened the political vacuum that Mali would fill. Weakened by Almoravid pressure in the eleventh century and by a long ecological decline, Wagadu fragmented into successor states including the Sosso kingdom, Mali's immediate predecessor.

spans.label: Founding & Expansion
spans.description: Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso Empire at the Battle of Kirina and united the Mandinka peoples, establishing the Kurukan Fuga oral constitution. The empire expanded to control the Bambuk and Bure gold fields and major trans-Saharan trade routes.

spans.label: Mali Golden Age
spans.description: Mansa Musa's legendary 1324 hajj displayed Mali's staggering wealth to the world, crashing the Egyptian gold market. Timbuktu became a major center of Islamic scholarship, and Mali's fame reached European mapmakers via the Catalan Atlas.

spans.label: Middle Period
spans.description: The empire maintained its territorial core but faced growing instability from succession disputes and pressure from neighboring peoples. Timbuktu's manuscript tradition and scholarly culture continued to flourish during this period.

spans.label: Mali Decline
spans.description: The rising Songhai Empire under Sonni Ali and Askia Muhammad absorbed Mali's eastern territories, including Timbuktu. Mali shrank to a rump state in the western Sahel before the Moroccan invasion of 1591 destabilized the entire region.

spans.label: The Long Mali Tail
spans.description: After the Moroccan destruction of Songhai, Mali survived as a small Keita kingdom around Kangaba and as the Kaabu confederation in the west. The political empire was essentially gone, but the oral tradition, the Manden charter, and the Mande cultural network outlived the dynasty by centuries.

events.label: Ghana Empire (Wagadu) flourishes
events.description: West Africa's first great gold empire, run by the Soninke people who called it Wagadu ("Ghana" was really the king's title, meaning warrior-king, that visiting Arabs mistook for the country's name). It got rich taxing gold on its way north.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Its likely capital, Koumbi Saleh (in modern southeastern Mauritania, about 200 miles north of present-day Bamako), may have held 40,000 to 50,000 people, making it one of the largest cities anywhere in West Africa. Archaeologists actually found two towns side by side: a Muslim merchants' quarter of stone houses and, a few miles off, the king's own town. The king alone was allowed to keep gold nuggets, while everyone else could trade only in gold dust, a clever way to keep prices from crashing.

events.label: Camel revolutionizes Sahara crossing
events.description: The desert ferry. Camels reached the northern Sahara from Arabia by way of Rome, and by the third and fourth centuries CE they finally let people cross the world's biggest hot desert on a regular schedule, something horses and donkeys simply could not survive.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: A camel could haul roughly 300 pounds about 15 to 18 miles a day, carrying around four times what a donkey could while needing far less water. Camels had reached Egypt as early as the ninth century BCE, but it took over a thousand years for the animal to spread west across North Africa and turn occasional desert travel into the steady, large-scale caravan trade that bankrolled Ghana, Mali, and Songhai.

events.label: Almoravid pressure on Ghana
events.description: The Almoravids were a militant Berber Muslim movement out of the western Sahara that overran Morocco and Spain in the same era. Older textbooks said they sacked Ghana's capital in 1076; historians now doubt that ever happened.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Two scholars, David Conrad and Humphrey Fisher, made the case in articles titled "The Conquest That Never Was," arguing the supposed sack was folklore read into much later Arabic sources rather than a real event. The dig at Koumbi Saleh shows no signs of the sudden burning or destruction a conquest would leave. What does seem clear is that the region converted to Islam around this time, suggesting Almoravid influence arrived through religion and pressure rather than a single battle.

events.label: Sosso kingdom under Sumanguru
events.description: After Ghana fell apart, a blacksmith-king named Sumanguru Kante built the Sosso kingdom into the region's strongman, swallowing old Ghana lands and pressing into Mandinka country. In the Sundiata epic he becomes the sorcerer-villain whose defeat gives birth to Mali.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Being both king and blacksmith was a fearsome combination in Mande culture, where ironworkers were thought to handle dangerous spiritual power. In the epic, Sumanguru owns a magical balafon (a wooden xylophone with gourd resonators); Sundiata's griot Balla Fasseke steals it and brings it to the Mandinka, said to be the origin of the Mande griot balafon tradition. An instrument claimed to be that very balafon, the Sosso Bala, is still guarded by the Kouyate griot family in Guinea and is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. The Sosso kingdom sat in what is now present-day Guinea and southwestern Mali.

events.label: Mandinka people of the Manden
events.description: The people who built Mali. The Mandinka (also called Malinke or Mandingo) farmed and herded along the upper Niger in a homeland they called the Manden, perfectly placed between the Bambuk gold fields to the west and the Niger trade routes to the east.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Today the Mandinka number around 15 million, one of Africa's largest ethnic groups, spread across Mali, Guinea, Senegal, The Gambia, and Guinea-Bissau. Their society was traditionally split into hereditary castes you married within: the freeborn (foro), the enslaved (jongo), and the artisans and praise-singers (nyamolo). Among the latter were the jeli, the griots, who acted as historian, royal counselor, court spokesman, and musician all at once, the living memory banks that carried the Sundiata epic down some eight centuries to the present.

events.label: Niger River as commercial highway
events.description: Mali's main street. The Niger does something no sensible river does: instead of running straight to the nearby Atlantic, it loops far north into the Sahel, brushes the desert at Timbuktu, then swings back south. That giant arc runs right through Mandinka country.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At about 2,600 miles (4,200 km) it is Africa's third-longest river, after the Nile and Congo. Its strangest feature is the Inner Niger Delta, a braided inland floodplain that swells to as much as 30,000 square kilometers (over 7 million acres) of seasonal wetland from September to December, even though it sits in the middle of dry country nowhere near the sea. The river is so leaky here that it loses roughly two-thirds of its flow to evaporation and seepage between Segou and Timbuktu, yet that very flooding is what feeds the rice and millet that fed the empire.

events.label: Sundiata Keita founds Mali Empire
events.description: A Mandinka prince who could barely walk as a child grew up to topple the Sosso king and stitch a scatter of clans into West Africa's biggest empire. He became the first mansa (emperor) of Mali.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His name is a tribute to his mother: "Sundiata" comes from Sogolon Djata, roughly "Sogolon's lion" (Djata, from jara, means lion in Mande), which is why he's nicknamed the Lion of Mali. Before his rise he spent years in exile, ending up in the kingdom of Mema, where its ruler Moussa Tounkara reportedly took him in, trained him in warfare, and considered grooming him as an heir. When the Sosso conquest of the Mandinka homeland reached its peak, envoys tracked Sundiata down in Mema and brought him home with an army to lead the revolt.

events.label: Battle of Kirina
events.description: The showdown that broke Sosso power: Sundiata's clan alliance crushed Sumanguru's army somewhere in what's now Mali's Koulikoro region, and the date is still taken as the empire's birthday.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: In the epic, Sundiata learns that Sumanguru's secret weakness is the rooster (the king's sacred animal), so he tips an arrow with a cock's spur and wounds him with it, breaking the sorcery that supposedly made the Sosso king invincible. Sumanguru isn't killed outright in most tellings; he flees the field and vanishes into the Koulikoro hills. The exact battle site has never been pinned down by archaeologists, so almost everything we know about Kirina comes from the oral epic rather than physical evidence.

events.label: Kurukan Fuga charter (Manden Charter)
events.description: A year after the war, Sundiata gathered the clans on an open plain and laid down the rules of the new empire out loud — an oral constitution that griots have recited ever since, never written down at the time.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The traditional meeting site sits near Kangaba in present-day Mali, where commemorative ceremonies are still held. UNESCO's 2009 listing summarizes the charter as a seven-chapter declaration promoting social peace across diverse groups, the inviolability of human life, education, food security, the ending of slave-raiding (razzia), and freedom of expression and trade. The full text we read today is a modern reconstruction assembled from several griot lineages in the late 1900s, so its provisions are an approximation rather than a verbatim record of 1236.

events.label: Niani established as capital
events.description: Sundiata set up his capital at Niani, a riverside town in the Mandinka heartland that would run the empire for roughly three centuries before fading.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Niani sits on the left bank of the Sankarani River (a tributary of the Niger) in what is now the Kankan region of eastern Guinea. Guinean-Polish archaeological missions dug there in 1965 and 1968, uncovering stone house foundations, a mosque's mihrab (the niche showing the direction of Mecca), and walls around the royal town, surrounded by separate hamlets for clans of smiths, fishermen, and traders. Even so, some scholars still doubt this site was truly the medieval capital, keeping Niani's identity one of West African archaeology's open questions.

events.label: Epic of Sundiata
events.description: Mali's national epic — the founding story carried by memory alone for centuries before anyone wrote it down. It's the main reason we know Sundiata's tale at all.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The best-known modern version is Djibril Tamsir Niane's Soundjata, ou l'Épopée mandingue, published in Paris by Présence Africaine in 1960 and based on the recitation of the griot Djeli Mamadou Kouyaté. G. D. Pickett translated it into English in 1965 as Sundiata: An Epic of Old Mali, the edition most readers outside West Africa encounter. Niane's text is a prose retelling, which means it smooths out the sung, rhythmic performance the griots actually deliver in front of an audience.

events.label: Griot (jeli) oral tradition
events.description: The griots — called jeli in the Mande languages — were a born-into-it caste of musicians, genealogists, and advisors who carried a noble family's entire history in their heads, no books required.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Griots married almost entirely within their own caste and trained their children from early childhood, which is how the memory survived across centuries. The jeli serving Mali's royal Keita line were the Kouyaté clan, whose tradition traces back to Balla Fasséké, remembered as the first griot. The English and French word "griot" likely entered European languages through Portuguese traders on the West African coast, though its exact origin is debated; the Mande speakers themselves never used it — their word is jeli, from a root tied to "blood," and the craft itself is jeliya.

events.label: Mande clan system
events.description: Mandinka society ran on named father-line clans, Keita, Konde, Traore, Camara, Kone, Diakite and more, each with its own inherited trade and rank. After founding Mali, Sundiata is said to have gathered the clans and laid down the rules that bound them together.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: That gathering produced the Kurukan Fuga (also called the Manden Charter), an oral constitution proclaimed around 1235 to 1236 on a granite clearing near Kangaba; the name itself means "clearing on the lateritic rock." UNESCO added it to its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2009, and a modern reconstruction of its articles was pieced together from griot memory at a 1998 workshop in Kankan, Guinea. One of its provisions formalized sanankuya, the "joking-cousin" bond that lets paired clans trade ritual insults, a social pressure-valve still alive across West Africa today.

events.label: Mali cavalry and horse trade
events.description: Mali's punch came from heavy cavalry — armored riders on horses shipped down across the Sahara from North Africa, a luxury so costly that owning warhorses was basically a club for the rich.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The reason the forest peoples to the south couldn't simply copy the tactic is biological: the tsetse fly, a biting insect of the wet equatorial belt, carries a parasite (trypanosomiasis, also called sleeping sickness) that kills horses outright. So the line where the flies stopped was also the line where cavalry warfare stopped. The price gap was steep elsewhere in West Africa too — in the later Oyo empire an imported horse cost at least twice the price of an enslaved person — and because horses bred poorly in the Sahel, the supply had to be constantly topped up from the north.

events.label: Mali controls Bambuk and Bure gold
events.description: Mali's wealth came out of the ground at two gold fields — Bambuk, between the Senegal and Falémé rivers, and Bure, on the upper Niger. Whoever taxed the caravans hauling that gold north got rich, and for a couple of centuries that was Mali.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Bambuk was sending gold north across the Sahara by at least the 700s, possibly far earlier; Bure opened up later, around the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The mining and shipping was run by a network of Muslim Soninke traders known as the Wangara, who fanned out into towns from Kano to Djenné. The miners kept the actual locations a fiercely guarded secret — Arab writers passed around tales of "silent barter," where traders left salt at a spot, banged drums, and withdrew so the goldminers could leave gold in exchange without ever showing their faces. Whether the dumb-barter story was literally true or a traveler's legend, the secrecy behind it was real.

events.label: Trans-Saharan salt-gold trade
events.description: The other half of the deal. Gold was everywhere in the south but salt was scarce, and people and cattle can't live without it. So caravans hauled slabs of Saharan rock salt south from mines like Taghaza and carried gold back north.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Taghaza lay about 489 miles (787 km) north-northwest of Timbuktu, and the traveler Ibn Battuta, who passed through in 1352, described a grim place where the houses and even the mosque were built from blocks of salt and roofed with camel skins. The salt was cut into thick slabs, two slung on each camel, and mined by enslaved laborers of the Berber Masufa tribe; merchants reportedly tacked on a transport markup close to 80 percent of the salt's value. Taghaza was finally abandoned in the late 1500s and replaced by the salt pans at Taoudenni.

events.label: Taghaza salt mines
events.description: Taghaza was the medieval Sahara's great salt mine, a brutal outpost roughly 500 miles (800 km) north of Timbuktu where slabs of rock salt were quarried straight out of a dry lakebed. In a region desperate for salt, those slabs were essentially money.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: When Ibn Battuta passed through in the 1350s, he noted that the village's houses and even its mosque were built from blocks of salt and roofed with camel skins. The salt came out of the ground in slabs laid flat "as if squared and stacked" underground, and a camel carried two of them. Further south salt was so scarce it traded weight-for-weight against gold — a camel-load that was nearly worthless in the desert could multiply in value many times over by the time it reached the Sahelian markets.

events.label: Islam spreads in Mali
events.description: Islam gradually spread among Mali's elite and merchant classes through trans-Saharan trade contacts, coexisting with traditional Mandinka religious practices. Mali developed a distinctive layered religious culture in which the royal family and major merchants were Muslim, the rural population mostly retained traditional beliefs, and the two systems intermingled in everyday life.

events.label: Mansa Uli's pilgrimage
events.description: Sundiata's son Mansa Uli became the first Mali ruler to make the pilgrimage to Mecca, kicking off a royal tradition that put the empire on the wider Muslim world's radar.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Sources put Uli's reign roughly 1255–1277, with the pilgrimage somewhere between 1260 and 1277 — the dates are fuzzy because the era is thinly documented. The 20th-century historian Nehemia Levtzion suggested Uli may have been the first mansa to push Mali's reach as far as Walata, a Saharan trade town, though later additions like Timbuktu and Gao are usually credited to his successors. The hajj was as much politics as piety: passing through Cairo put a West African king face to face with the rulers and scholars of the eastern Mediterranean.

events.label: Mansa Sakura
events.description: Sakura was a freed slave-soldier who grabbed the throne during a stretch of dynastic chaos — and somehow ruled as a legitimate mansa anyway, expanding Mali eastward toward Gao before he was killed coming home from Mecca.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The reign dates (about 1285–1300) come from the French colonial scholar Maurice Delafosse's estimates, not hard records. The great Arab historian Ibn Khaldun, who covered Sakura in more detail than most early mansas and called him a mighty ruler, says he was murdered at Tajura — a town about 12 miles (19 km) east of Tripoli on the Libyan coast — while returning from the pilgrimage. A competing oral tradition says he was instead killed by Qu (Kon Mamadi), a grandson of Sundiata, who then took the throne and returned power to the royal Keita line.

events.label: Abu Bakr II's Atlantic expedition
events.description: A famous story, told by Mansa Musa in Cairo and written down by the Egyptian scholar al-Umari, has Musa's predecessor sailing a fleet of 2,000 ships west into the Atlantic to find the ocean's far edge — and vanishing.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The name "Abu Bakr II" is almost certainly a mistake: the 19th-century translator Baron de Slane misread Ibn Khaldun and turned a name in Musa's family tree into a supposed king. No Mansa Abu Bakr II ever reigned; the predecessor was most likely Mansa Muhammad (Muhammad ibn Qu), and al-Umari's text never actually names him. The tale reached al-Umari third-hand — Musa told an emir, who told al-Umari — and in the original version the first scouting trip was 200 ships, only one of which came back. No accepted evidence of pre-Columbian African contact with the Americas has ever turned up, so historians file the whole thing under legend.

events.label: Mansa Musa
events.description: Mali's tenth ruler and its most famous, Mansa Musa ran the empire at its absolute peak — Atlantic coast to the Niger Bend, an area about the size of Western Europe. He's the man behind every "richest person ever" listicle, though that ranking is more clickbait than history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Modern historians actually doubt the old story that Musa's predecessor was a "Mansa Abu Bakr II" who sailed off into the Atlantic and never came back. That name traces to a 19th-century mistranslation of the Arab historian Ibn Khaldun by Baron de Slane; in the original Arabic, Abu Bakr is named only as the ancestor of Musa's family line, not as a king. Musa's real predecessor was a ruler called Muhammad, and Musa most likely took the throne in 1312 (some sources say 1307).

events.label: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca
events.description: In 1324 Musa set out across the Sahara for Mecca with a caravan so loaded with gold it became the stuff of legend — and accidentally rewrote how the rest of the world saw West Africa. By the time he came home, the Islamic world knew Mali existed and European mapmakers were drawing its king.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Egyptian writer al-Umari, our main source, listed an entourage of 8,000 courtiers, 12,000 servants, and 100 camels each carrying gold dust. The caravan crossed the desert in pilgrim's white but Musa's people are said to have dressed in fine brocade. Along the way Musa gave gold to the poor in every city he passed, and Mali's hajj route was a real overland slog of several months through salt-mining outposts before it ever reached Egypt.

events.label: Musa crashes Egyptian gold market
events.description: Musa handed out gold in Cairo so freely — to officials, scholars, shopkeepers, the poor — that he flooded the market and sent the price of gold crashing for years. It's one of the best-documented examples of a one-man monetary shock in the pre-modern world.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before he even settled in, Musa reportedly sent the Egyptian sultan a gift of 50,000 gold dinars. The mithqal (a standard gold weight) fell below 25 dirhams (silver coins) during his stay and stayed depressed afterward. Cairo's merchants, sensing easy marks, overcharged his retinue so badly that Musa ran short and had to borrow money at steep interest for the trip home — and some of those creditors trailed him all the way back to Mali to collect.

events.label: Mansa Musa in Cairo
events.description: Musa spent about three months in Cairo in the summer of 1324 as a guest of the Mamluk sultan — and it's almost entirely because of this stopover that we know what we know about him. Egyptian and Syrian writers actually laid eyes on his court; nobody outside Mali wrote down the rest of his reign in nearly the same detail.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Al-Umari (full name Shihab al-Din al-Umari) never met Musa himself; he gathered his account from Cairo officials about twelve years after the visit, who were reportedly still gossiping about it. The famous friction was over court protocol: Musa balked at the customary prostration before the sultan, and the standoff was only resolved when he agreed to bow to God rather than to the throne. His host was al-Nasir Muhammad, a Mamluk ruler twice deposed and twice restored who held power, on and off, for more than half a century.

events.label: Djinguereber Mosque built
events.description: Timbuktu's biggest and oldest of three great mosques, built of mud brick bristling with palm-wood beams. It still works as a mosque today, nearly seven centuries on, which means it has been re-plastered by hand after almost every rainy season since the 1320s.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tradition credits the design to al-Sahili, an Andalusian (Muslim Spain) scholar-architect Mansa Musa reportedly brought back from his pilgrimage — and the chronicler Ibn Khaldun says he was paid a staggering 12,000 mithqals of gold dust for the work (a mithqal was a small coin-weight of gold, so this was a fortune). Modern scholars now doubt the al-Sahili story, arguing the Sudano-Sahelian mud-brick style grew out of older Saharan and West African building traditions rather than a single imported genius. The mosque is part of the Timbuktu UNESCO World Heritage Site, which was listed as endangered after the 2012 jihadist occupation.

events.label: Timbuktu becomes center of learning
events.description: After Mansa Musa came home from his gold-soaked pilgrimage to Mecca, he turned a dusty Tuareg watering hole on the desert's edge into an imperial showpiece — and within a few generations Timbuktu had become one of the Islamic world's real centers of learning, packed with scholars, copyists, and students.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The city sits about 8 miles (13 km) north of the Niger River, just close enough to plug into river trade and just far enough into the sand to control the caravan routes — a sweet spot where Saharan salt met Sahelian gold. At its peak the resident scholar population ran to several hundred, with a few thousand students drifting through at any given time, though the whole city probably never topped 50,000 people. The name likely comes from a Tuareg phrase tied to a woman, possibly an enslaved one, said to have minded the original wells — though that origin story is folk etymology and may not be reliable.

events.label: Sankoré Mosque and University
events.description: The mosque on Timbuktu's north side that became the beating heart of the city's intellectual life. Modern writers love to call its attached school "Sankoré University," but it had no central administration, no enrollment, and no diplomas — just master scholars and the students who clustered around them.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The teaching worked on a personal apprenticeship model: a student attached himself to a particular master (a shaykh), worked through one text under his eye, earned a certificate (an ijaza) saying he'd finished it, then moved on to the next master — and his stack of ijazas was his whole resume. Local tradition holds that a wealthy woman financed the mosque, though accounts disagree on whether she was Mandinka or Tuareg. When an imam rebuilt the inner sanctuary in the 1570s–80s, he reportedly gave its courtyard the exact dimensions of the Kaaba in Mecca, which he had measured on his own pilgrimage.

events.label: Sidi Yahya Mosque
events.description: The third of Timbuktu's great mud-brick mosques, finished in the mid-fifteenth century and named for its first imam. Local lore held that its main door must stay sealed until the day before the end of the world — so for centuries nobody opened it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The mosque was built between roughly 1400 and 1440, and Sidi Yahya al-Tadelsi was appointed its first imam in 1441. The legend protected that door for almost six hundred years, until July 2012, when fighters from Ansar Dine (a hardline group tied to al-Qaeda) smashed it open during their occupation of the city, saying they wanted to "destroy the mystery" because it clashed with their austere reading of Islam. UNESCO and local woodworkers restored the doorway in 2013 after the militants were driven out.

events.label: Catalan Atlas depicts Mansa Musa
events.description: In 1375 a Mallorcan mapmaker drew Mansa Musa enthroned in the African corner of the Catalan Atlas, gold nugget in hand — the first time a sub-Saharan African ruler showed up on a European map. Fifty years after the hajj, Mali's reputation had soaked all the way into Christian Europe.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The atlas was made by Cresques Abraham (often called Abraham Cresques), working with his son Jehuda, on six leaves of vellum painted with real gold and silver. Musa sits on the second panel holding a golden orb, and his caption reads roughly: "This black lord is called Musse Melly... the richest and noblest king of all these lands, on account of the abundance of gold that is gathered in his land." It was likely produced as a royal gift bound for the French court.

events.label: Ibn Battuta visits Mali
events.description: The Moroccan globetrotter who actually showed up and took notes. Ibn Battuta spent about eight months in Mali in 1352–53, and his report is the single best eyewitness account of the empire we have — detailed, opinionated, and not shy about what he disliked.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: His full travel book carries the wonderful title "A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities and the Marvels of Travelling" — usually just called the Rihla ("Journey"). He griped that Mansa Suleyman was a stingy host, sending him a welcome gift of only three loaves of bread, a piece of fried beef, and a calabash of sour milk. He also recorded river-dwellers hunting hippos along the Niger and leaving great heaps of their bones, and was scandalized that Mali's women moved freely in public unveiled — his exact complaints are part of why historians trust the rest: a flatterer he was not.

events.label: Mansa Suleyman
events.description: Musa's brother Suleyman held the empire together for nearly two decades and kept funding Islamic scholarship — but went down in history as a tightwad next to his dazzling brother. He's mostly remembered because a famous traveler showed up to write it all down.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ibn Battuta — a Moroccan globetrotter from the Marinid sultanate — visited around 1352 and left the most detailed firsthand portrait of Mali at its height. He arrived in the middle of a palace scandal: Suleyman accused his chief wife, Qasa, of plotting a coup with an exiled royal, jailed her, and replaced her with another wife, Banju. The drama outlasted him — Suleyman died around 1359-1360, his son ruled only about nine months, and civil war broke out soon after.

events.label: Cowrie shell currency
events.description: Cowrie shells from the Maldives in the Indian Ocean served as everyday small-change currency throughout the Mali Empire, while gold dust was used for larger transactions. The cowries traveled overland through Egypt and across the Sahara — one of the longer commodity chains of the medieval world economy.

events.label: Great Mosque of Djenné
events.description: The Great Mosque of Djenné is a mountain of mud — the largest building on Earth made from sun-dried clay brick. The original went up in Mali's heyday in this distinctive Sahelian style, all rounded walls bristling with wooden beams.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The mosque you see today is not medieval: the French oversaw a full rebuild in 1907 under Ismaila Traoré, head of Djenné's masons' guild, using forced labor. Mud architecture melts in the rain, so the whole town turns out every year before the rains for the crepissage — a festival where residents re-plaster the entire building by hand, music playing and griots (oral historians) entertaining the workers. Djenné and its mosque were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.

events.label: Djenné-Djenno archaeology
events.description: A buried city next door to medieval Djenné that, when archaeologists finally dug it in the late 1970s, turned out to be older than the empire of Ghana itself — proof that West Africans were building real cities long before any caravan from the north showed up.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Husband-and-wife archaeologists Roderick and Susan McIntosh excavated the mound between 1977 and 1981, tracing continuous settlement from roughly 250 BCE to about 1400 CE, with a peak population near 20,000. The site is famous for its terracotta figurines of people and animals — so prized that many had been looted and sold to Western collectors before the digs even began. Strikingly, the city seems to have grown without a king or palace at its center, hinting that complex urban life in the region did not require a top-down state to spark it. Djenné-Djenno is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.label: Timbuktu manuscript tradition
events.description: From the late 1300s on, Timbuktu's scholars copied, wrote, and hoarded manuscripts on everything from astronomy to law to poetry — by the hundreds of thousands. They are the single biggest body of pre-colonial sub-Saharan African writing, and their existence demolishes the old myth that the region had no written tradition.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Most of the corpus survived not in any grand archive but in private family libraries, handed down for generations. When jihadist groups seized Timbuktu in 2012, a librarian named Abdel Kader Haidara organized a clandestine eight-month rescue: hundreds of packers and couriers spirited more than 350,000 manuscripts out of the city in metal footlockers, mule carts, and 4x4s, smuggling them past checkpoints by road and down the Niger by boat. By the time French troops arrived in January 2013, the militants had managed to burn only around 4,000 of the nearly 400,000 works — the vast majority were saved.

events.label: Astronomy in Timbuktu
events.description: Timbuktu scholars produced manuscripts on astronomy and mathematics, including treatises on celestial movements, planetary tables, and the determination of prayer times. The intellectual lineage was directly continuous with Islamic Golden Age astronomical scholarship, with Timbuktu working from the same Arabic-language tradition as Cairo and Baghdad.

events.label: Medical scholarship in Mali
events.description: Malian scholars compiled medical texts combining Islamic medical knowledge from the Avicenna tradition with indigenous West African herbal and surgical practice. Recovered Timbuktu manuscripts include treatises on ophthalmology, pharmacology, and obstetrics.

events.label: Sonni Ali captures Timbuktu
events.description: Sonni Ali, Songhai's warrior-king, took Timbuktu from Mali in 1468 and made it the empire's second city. He had little patience for the town's holy men and dealt with them harshly — which is why Timbuktu's later writers remembered him as a monster.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Five years after Timbuktu, Sonni Ali turned on Djenné, the great walled trading city of the Inner Niger Delta. Legend says he besieged it for seven years, seven months, and seven days before starving it into surrender in 1473 — and then, in sharp contrast to Timbuktu, spared everyone because he admired how hard they had fought. He drowned crossing a river in 1492, the same year Columbus reached the Caribbean. In Songhai memory he is a founding hero on the order of Sundiata; in Timbuktu's Arabic chronicles he is a tyrant — and both were written down by people with reasons to remember him their way.

events.label: Songhai Empire eclipses Mali
events.description: Mali's old vassal on the Niger Bend grew up and ate its master. Over roughly a century the Songhai Empire, run from the river city of Gao, swallowed Mali's eastern provinces one by one until Mali was just its western Mandinka homeland again.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At its peak under Askia Muhammad, Songhai was the largest empire West Africa ever produced — bigger than Mali at its height — stretching from the Atlantic in modern Senegal east to Hausaland (the cluster of trading city-states in what is now northern Nigeria), where Songhai armies hit Gobir, Katsina, and Zaria and forced wealthy Kano to pay heavy tribute. Its northern edge reached the brutal Saharan salt mines of Taghaza. The whole structure held together for barely a century before a Moroccan invasion in 1591 shattered it.

events.label: Askia Muhammad consolidates Songhai
events.description: When Sonni Ali died, his top general shoved aside the heir and took the throne as Askia Muhammad. He flipped the script — where Sonni Ali sneered at Islam, Askia built his whole rule on it, and repaired the scholarly community his predecessor had gutted.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: On his 1497–98 pilgrimage to Mecca he wrangled the title "Caliph of the Sudan" (sudan being the Arabic word for the West African Sahel) from the puppet Abbasid caliph in Cairo — a religious rubber-stamp no Mali ruler had ever bothered to collect. Back home he leaned on imported Maghrebi scholars; one of them, al-Maghili, wrote him the famous "Replies to Askia," a written legal Q&A on how a Muslim king should govern that doubled as propaganda branding Sonni Ali's dynasty as un-Islamic. Askia ruled until 1528, when his own son overthrew him; he had reportedly gone blind by then.

events.label: Kola nut trade
events.description: Mali's southern provinces controlled the trade in kola nuts from the forest regions of modern Guinea and Ivory Coast, where they were prized as caffeinated stimulants and used in religious and social ceremonies across the Sahel. Kola nuts traveled north into the Sahara and across to North Africa, becoming one of Mali's most important non-gold exports.

events.label: Niger River commerce
events.description: The Niger River was Mali's moving highway — a watery main street where flat-bottomed pirogue canoes and big freight boats hauled gold, slabs of salt, copper, dried fish, and grain between the river towns of Niani, Djenné, Timbuktu, and Gao.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Niger is the third-longest river in Africa, running about 2,600 miles (4,180 km) on a strange boomerang loop that rises near the Atlantic coast, swings north into the edge of the Sahara, then bends back south to the sea. The salt-for-gold math along it was brutal: a roughly 200-pound (90 kg) block of salt floated down from Timbuktu to Djenné could double in value, and salt sometimes traded close to its own weight in gold. River canoes did the heavy lifting that camels couldn't — a single freight boat moved far more cargo than any caravan.

events.label: Traditional Mandinka religion
events.description: Despite royal conversion to Islam, most Malians practiced traditional religions centered on ancestor veneration, spirit worship, and secret societies (such as the Komo) that regulated community life and initiation. The royal Islam of the court coexisted with village ritual life rather than displacing it, producing the layered religious culture that still characterizes much of West Africa.

events.label: Marabout scholars in Mali
events.description: Muslim holy men called marabouts — a Berber-influenced West African term for Sufi-influenced scholar-clerics — served as teachers, judges, healers, and amulet-makers throughout the empire. They blended Islamic scholarship with local spiritual traditions and were the connective tissue between elite court Islam and rural religious practice.

events.label: Al-Sahili, architect from Granada
events.description: Musa came home in 1325 with a souvenir of a very different kind: Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, a poet-architect from Granada he'd recruited in Cairo. Mali tradition made him the father of Sahelian brick architecture, but the real story is more modest.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The mud-brick building tradition the Sahel is famous for was already ancient by al-Sahili's day — monumental mud architecture at sites like Djenné-Djenno goes back to the early first millennium CE, long before any Andalusian arrived. What al-Sahili most plausibly contributed was Andalusian decorative touches and supervision of specific commissions; Ibn Khaldun, who names him as a genuine figure at Musa's court, credits him with the Timbuktu mosque work and a 12,000-mithqal (gold-weight) payment.

events.label: Ahmed Baba al-Timbukti
events.description: The most celebrated scholar Timbuktu ever produced — a jurist who wrote more than forty books and whose biographical dictionary of legal scholars stayed a standard reference for centuries. He's also remembered for arguing, in detail, that enslaving West African Muslims broke Islamic law.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: After Moroccan troops occupied Timbuktu in 1591 they hauled Ahmed Baba off to Marrakesh, jailing him before forcing him to stay and teach for years; he wasn't allowed home until 1607. His most famous line, supposedly delivered to the Moroccan sultan, was that the soldiers had stolen more than 1,600 books from him — and that this was the smallest library among all his relatives, a one-sentence glimpse of just how book-rich Timbuktu's scholarly families were. His treatise on the slave trade, the Mi'raj al-Su'ud, drew on a century of Timbuktu legal thinking to declare much of the trans-Saharan trade illegitimate. Timbuktu's main manuscript institute today bears his name.

events.label: Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-Fattash
events.description: Almost everything we know in detail about Mali and Songhai comes from two Arabic chronicles written in seventeenth-century Timbuktu. They're the hinge between the jeli's spoken memory and the written historical record.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Mahmud Kati supposedly began the Tarikh al-Fattash in 1519 at age 51, and his sons and grandsons carried the work forward to around 1665 — one grandson, Ibn al-Mukhtar, did much of the actual writing. The companion chronicle, the Tarikh al-Sudan by Abd al-Rahman al-Sadi, came a little later and rivals it in scope. Both run the Songhai story from Sonni Ali up to the Moroccan conquest of 1599. Modern scholarship has gotten complicated: the standard 1913 French edition of the Fattash turns out to have stitched two different manuscripts together.

events.label: Sudano-Sahelian architecture
events.description: Mali's distinctive mud-brick architectural style, with timber beam reinforcement protruding from the walls and conical buttressed minarets, became the defining aesthetic of West African Islamic architecture. The protruding beams (called toron) function as built-in scaffolding for the regular re-plastering that mud-brick walls require after each rainy season.

events.label: West African iron smelting
events.description: Mandinka blacksmiths produced high-quality iron tools and weapons in clan-monopolized smithies. Numu (blacksmith) clans held a revered and slightly feared social position in Mali's caste system, considered to handle dangerous spiritual power along with metallurgy. West African iron technology had developed independently more than a thousand years before Mali emerged.

events.label: Moroccan invasion at Tondibi
events.description: On March 13, 1591, a Moroccan force of about 4,000 muskets and cannons smashed a Songhai cavalry army many times its size at Tondibi, on the Niger just north of Gao. In roughly two hours, the guns broke the lance-and-saber charges that had ruled Sahelian warfare for centuries — and the great western Sahel empires were finished.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Moroccan force was a lean column of 1,500 light cavalry and 2,500 arquebusiers (men with the matchlock long gun called an arquebus). The Songhai king Askia Ishaq II reportedly tried to stampede a herd of cattle into the Moroccan line to disrupt it, but the volleys and cannon noise turned the cattle back into his own troops. The Tarikh al-Sudan, a Timbuktu chronicle written decades later, records that some Songhai soldiers, bound by a code of honor, sat down on their shields rather than flee and were cut down where they sat.

events.label: Saadian dynasty of Morocco
events.description: The Saadians were Morocco's ruling dynasty (claiming descent from the Prophet Muhammad), and under Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur they turned a stunning 1578 victory over Portugal into the war chest that paid for the gamble across the Sahara. Al-Mansur wanted one thing above all: West Africa's gold, seized at the source instead of bought through middlemen.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: At the 1578 battle near Ksar el-Kebir — nicknamed the Battle of the Three Kings because three rulers died that day — the boy-king Sebastian I of Portugal was killed, leaving no heir and triggering the crisis that let Spain swallow Portugal in 1580. Al-Mansur (whose title means 'the Victorious') filled his treasury by ransoming thousands of captured Portuguese nobles. A restless schemer, he corresponded with Queen Elizabeth I about a joint strike on Spain and even floated plans to seize Spanish colonies in the Americas. He died of plague in 1603, and within decades the Saadians were gone, replaced by the Alawi dynasty that still rules Morocco today.

events.label: Judar Pasha leads Saharan crossing
events.description: Judar Pasha led the desert march that conquered Songhai — and he was an unlikely choice: a Spanish-born castrated slave raised in the sultan's household. Half his army died crossing the Sahara, yet the survivors' guns still won at Tondibi, after which he occupied Timbuktu and Gao without ever truly controlling them.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: He was born Diego de Guevara in Cuevas del Almanzora in Castile, captured by slave-raiders as a child, castrated, and known in Morocco for his startling blue eyes. When he finally returned home in 1599, his caravan carried thirty camel-loads of gold that one English merchant valued at £600,000 — a colossal sum for the era. His own end was grim: he was executed in December 1606, strangled amid the dynastic civil war that tore Morocco apart after al-Mansur's death.

events.label: Arma military caste in Timbuktu
events.description: The conquerors stayed and went local. The Arma — descendants of the Moroccan musketeers, the name from al-rumat, 'the marksmen' — married into Niger Bend families and hardened into a proud hereditary warrior caste that ran Timbuktu, Gao, and Djenné as their own for generations, the tie to distant Marrakesh fading to almost nothing.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: They governed through a polity historians call the Pashalik of Timbuktu, a province led by pashas the soldiers themselves elected once Morocco's grip slipped after al-Mansur's death in 1603. Numbering perhaps 2,000 to 3,000 fighters at first, they kept marrying only among themselves and styled themselves a race apart — locally nicknamed Gakory, 'white body' in the Songhay language, a nod to their North African ancestry. By the mid-1600s the link to Morocco was purely ceremonial, and the Arma ruled as independent lords.

events.label: Keita kingdom of Kangaba
events.description: When the imperial center fell apart, the Keita royal family did the symbolic thing and went home — back to Kangaba, the upstream village their dynasty came from before the empire ever existed. They've held the chiefship there ever since.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Kangaba was already loaded with meaning before the retreat: it sits on the Niani-area plain of Kurukan Fuga where Sundiata Keita is said to have proclaimed the Manden Charter after his 1235 victory at Krina. The town's full Mande name is Kaba. After Sundiata's reign the Keita capital function had drifted elsewhere, so the seventeenth-century return was less a new settlement than a homecoming to the clan's deepest root — the one place where being a Keita still meant something even after the empire stopped paying out.

events.label: Kaabu confederation
events.description: Out west, in what is now Guinea-Bissau and its neighbors, a cluster of Mande kingdoms called Kaabu kept the Mali political idea alive for over two centuries after the empire itself was gone — until a Muslim Fula army wiped it out in a single apocalyptic siege in 1867.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Kaabu's warrior aristocracy, the Nyancho, traced descent back to the Mande heartland and ran the federation through a rotating kingship among its constituent provinces. The final siege at Kansala carries a famous legend: the last ruler, Mansaba Janke Waali (also spelled Dianke Walli), reportedly prophesied that he would be Kaabu's last king. Convinced his roughly 25,000-strong force could not beat the Imamate of Futa Jallon, the story goes that he let the enemy pour into the fortress, then had his sons torch the city's gunpowder magazines — blowing up attackers and defenders together. The Mandinka name for the battle, Turban Keloo, means the war of annihilation.

events.label: Kamabolon ceremony at Kangaba
events.description: Every seventh year the people of Kangaba re-roof a small painted mud sanctuary called the Kamabolon, and on the roofless night before the new roof goes on, senior griots recite the official, full-length Sundiata epic inside it. It is the closest thing the Mande world has to a scripture-reading.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The whole event runs about five days and works as a society-wide reset: a fresh age-group of young men does the ritual labor of repairing the walls and building the roof, so the ceremony also inaugurates them into adulthood. The Keita clan and griots carrying the Diabate surname are the recognized keepers and organizers. Anthropologists who documented the 1997 ceremony noted it is often called the only epic in the world transmitted purely orally yet performed in a fixed ceremonial setting — the recitation is also an occasion to settle disputes and to foretell what the next seven years will bring.

events.label: Niani's decline as capital
events.description: Niani, the capital Ibn Battuta described in the 1350s, shrank to nothing — and here is the strange part: archaeologists still cannot agree on where it actually was. A great medieval city more or less erased itself from the map.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The long-standing candidate is the village of Niani in modern Guinea, an identification first proposed by French colonial scholars in 1923. But radiocarbon dating there shows a conspicuous gap in occupation across the late thirteenth to early fifteenth centuries — exactly the empire's heyday — and several twenty-first-century scholars have now firmly rejected it as the capital. Some re-readings of Ibn Battuta even place the royal seat far to the west, toward the upper Gambia. The likely culprit for the vanishing is the building material: unfired mud brick dissolves back into the soil within a few rainy seasons once people stop re-plastering it, so an abandoned Sahelian city can melt away in a couple of generations.

events.label: Mansa Musa in European imagination
events.description: Mansa Musa's debut on the 1375 Catalan Atlas — enthroned, crowned, holding up a lump of gold — became the template for how Europe pictured a rich African king for the next several centuries. The trouble was that everyone read the gold as his and missed the trade system behind it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The atlas was made on Majorca by Cresques Abraham, a Jewish master mapmaker, who drew Musa cross-legged on a golden throne with a European-style orb and scepter and a gold nugget in his raised hand. The caption calls him "Musse Melly," sovereign of the land of the Black people, and declares him "the richest and noblest of all these lands due to the abundance of gold that is extracted from his lands" — a line that fixed the gold-king image in the European mind generations before any European had set foot in his empire.

events.label: Timbuktu as European myth
events.description: For Europeans, Timbuktu became shorthand for the unreachable ends of the earth — a fabled city of gold no Westerner had managed to reach and survive. When one finally did, in 1828, he found a dusty clay town that made the legend look ridiculous.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: In 1826 the Paris Société de Géographie dangled a 10,000-franc prize for the first European to reach Timbuktu and come back alive. A Scottish officer, Gordon Laing, got there in 1826 but was murdered on the way out, so the prize fell to the Frenchman René Caillié, who arrived disguised as a Muslim pilgrim in April 1828, lingered about two weeks, and crossed the Sahara home. He collected the francs and was made a Knight of the Legion of Honour — and his deflating account of an ordinary mud town was initially met with disbelief by audiences who preferred the myth.

events.label: Leo Africanus describes Timbuktu
events.description: Leo Africanus — born al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Wazzan in Granada around 1494, captured by Christian pirates and converted in Rome — published his Description of Africa in 1526 in Italian, providing the most influential European-readable account of sixteenth-century West Africa. His chapters on Timbuktu, written from his 1510 visit, shaped European perceptions of the Sahel for two hundred years.

events.label: Atlantic slave trade shadow
events.description: The other blow to Mali came from the ocean, not the desert. As European traders fortified the West African coast, the long-distance trade that had once flowed north across the Sahara to Mali's markets swung south toward the sea — a slow reorientation that hollowed out what the Moroccan invasion had wrecked.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The anchor of this new coastal commerce was already old: the Portuguese built Elmina Castle (Castelo de São Jorge da Mina, 'St. George of the Mine') on the Gold Coast of present-day Ghana in 1482 — the first European trading fort south of the Sahara and the oldest surviving European building in sub-Saharan Africa. Its stones were shipped pre-cut from Portugal and assembled on the spot, an early prefabricated building. The Dutch seized it in 1637, and over the next two centuries it became one of the grimmest hubs of the Atlantic slave trade, a 'door of no return' for enslaved Africans.

events.label: Manden Charter inscribed by UNESCO
events.description: In 2009 UNESCO put the Manden Charter on its list of humanity's intangible cultural heritage — official global recognition for a constitution that has no original copy because it lived for nearly eight centuries entirely in the memory of griots.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The reconstructed text, as published by the griot Siriman Kouyate, runs to 44 edicts grouped under social organization, property, the environment, and personal duties. Among them: a ban on raiding people into slavery, a right of refuge, food-security provisions, and protections for the natural world — which is why it is often described as one of the oldest constitutional and human-rights documents anywhere. The UNESCO citation frames its preamble as advocating social peace in diversity and the inviolability of the human person. The listing carries no legal force; it is recognition, not law.

events.label: Timbuktu manuscripts rescued, 2012–13
events.description: When jihadists seized Timbuktu in 2012 and started burning manuscripts, a local librarian named Abdel Kader Haidara quietly organized a smuggling ring to spirit the city's medieval books south to safety — by trunk, donkey cart, and canoe.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Over roughly nine months, Haidara's couriers moved an estimated 350,000 manuscripts out of about 45 libraries and more than 400 miles (about 640 km) downriver to Bamako, often traveling at night in rented 4x4s carrying two or three locked metal footlockers at a time, with manuscripts also hidden under car seats and blankets. When militants torched part of the Ahmed Baba Institute as French and Malian forces closed in during early 2013, the great bulk of the corpus had already escaped. The texts are not just Qur'ans — they cover astronomy, law, medicine, mathematics, and poetry, the working library of a centuries-old scholarly city.
